intro: People often say a leader is far left or a party is center-right. But what do those words really measure? This unit gives you tools to compare political systems with care. You will start with the one-line spectrum from 1789, then add a second axis, test the horseshoe idea, and see how labels shift from the United States to Europe, Latin America and Asia.

Next you will follow countries that moved toward democracy: Portugal and Spain in the 1970s, South Korea and Taiwan in the 1980s and 1990s, Eastern Europe in 1989, Chile in 1990 and South Africa in 1994. You will also learn how political scientists describe democracies weakening, and why they watch courts, the press and the rule of law under governments of the left and the right.

By the end you will be able to place ideas on a model and explain its limits, compare paths to democracy with evidence, and name warning signs fairly. You will practice using the same test for every side, which is one of the strongest habits a citizen can build.
bigQuestion: How can we compare political systems fairly, and what helps democracy grow or weaken?

timeline.t: Seating in France's National Assembly gives us the terms left and right
Japan's Liberal Democratic Party forms and begins decades of leadership
A military coup in Chile overthrows Salvador Allende
Portugal's Carnation Revolution begins Huntington's third wave
Spain holds its first free elections after Franco
South Korea's June Democracy Movement wins direct elections; Taiwan lifts martial law
Chileans vote No to more years of Pinochet's rule
Solidarity wins in Poland and the Berlin Wall opens
South Africa holds its first election open to all races
Taiwan holds its first direct presidential election
Levitsky and Ziblatt publish How Democracies Die on democratic backsliding

words.d: a range of positions laid out along a line from one end to the other
a system or view where power is concentrated in rulers who limit personal freedom and do not face free elections
a view that wants the smallest possible role for the state in both the economy and personal life
the idea that the far left and far right resemble each other more than either resembles the center
a system in which the government provides a broad safety net paid for by taxes
a country that holds elections but where one party wins them again and again for decades
a sudden seizure of government power, often by the military
Huntington's name for the spread of democracy that began in Portugal in 1974
a change to democracy in which the old rulers keep some power or protections as they step aside
the gradual weakening of democratic rules and rights, often by elected leaders
the principle that everyone, including leaders, must obey the same laws
unwritten habits and expectations that guide how people in power behave

test.q: Where do the political terms left and right come from?
test.why: Members sat on the left or right of the hall in 1789.

test.q: What does the vertical axis on a common two-axis grid measure?
test.why: The grid adds a measure of state control over personal life.

test.q: Which pair best shows why one line is not enough?
choices: Stalin's USSR and Pinochet's Chile: opposite economics, both authoritarian
test.why: Their economics differed but both ruled without free elections.

test.q: What do critics of horseshoe theory argue?
choices: The far left and far right had opposite goals
test.why: Critics stress the very different aims of the two extremes.

test.q: Which country pairs high taxes and broad services with mostly private companies?
test.why: Sweden is the chapter's case of social democracy.

test.q: Why is Singapore hard to place on a single line?
choices: It mixes open markets and low taxes with large public housing and firm state control
It has no elections at all
test.why: Its mix of features does not fit one point.

test.q: In the United States, liberal usually means favoring an active government. What does it often mean in much of Europe?
test.why: Labels shift by country; European liberals often favor markets.

choices: Chilean economists trained at the University of Chicago
test.why: They shaped free-market policy under Pinochet.

test.q: Which event began Huntington's third wave?
test.why: Huntington dated the third wave from Portugal in 1974.

test.q: What did Spain's king do during the 1981 coup attempt?
choices: He appeared on television and backed the constitution
test.why: The king's support for the constitution helped the coup fail.

test.q: Which statement about Taiwan is correct?
choices: It lifted martial law in 1987 and held its first direct presidential election in 1996
It never held a direct election
test.why: Taiwan changed step by step between 1987 and 1996.

test.q: What did F. W. de Klerk do in 1990?
choices: Unbanned the ANC and released Nelson Mandela
test.why: These steps opened the negotiations that ended apartheid.

choices: Elected leaders gradually weakening the rules that let voters remove them
test.why: Backsliding is slow weakening, often by elected governments.

test.q: Which is a sign of democratic strength rather than a warning light?
choices: A leader loses in court and obeys the ruling
Election rules changed by the ruling party alone
test.why: Obeying a court ruling shows the rule of law working.

test.q: Why does the unit discuss both Venezuela and Hungary?
choices: To show backsliding described under both left- and right-leaning governments
test.why: Applying the same test to both sides is the unit's key habit.

write.prompt: Which matters more for a lasting democracy: pressure from ordinary citizens or choices made by leaders in power? Use at least two cases from this unit, such as South Korea, Spain, Chile or South Africa, and explain your claim with evidence.
tips: Name each case and give a specific date or fact.
Show the strongest version of the other side before you answer it.
Use unit terms like transition, plebiscite or negotiated transition correctly.
Apply the same standard to governments of the left and the right.
